briefing.headline: Every API speaks this. You should too.
body: JSON is the format that APIs use to send data — requests you make, responses you receive, configuration files, the module files powering this course. When Claude returns a catch log structure, when the Anthropic API responds, when your app stores settings — it's JSON.
This is a short module. JSON is simple. The goal isn't mastery, it's fluency: read it without hesitating, write it correctly, spot errors fast. That's it.

reference.title: JSON rules
reference.content: Keys must be strings in double quotes. Strings must use double quotes (not single). No trailing commas after the last item. No comments. Numbers, booleans (true/false), and null are unquoted. These are the four most common parse errors.

reference.title: Parse and stringify in JavaScript
Validate JSON from the terminal
reference.content:
# Check if a file is valid JSON
python3 -m json.tool data.json

# Pretty-print a JSON file
cat data.json | python3 -m json.tool

# With jq (if installed via brew)
cat data.json | jq .

reference.title: "Unexpected token" or "Unexpected end"
reference.content: Your JSON is malformed. Common causes: trailing comma on last item, single quotes instead of double, unquoted key. Paste the JSON into jsonlint.com — it highlights the exact line.

reference.title: "Circular structure" on JSON.stringify
reference.content: The object you're trying to stringify references itself — a DOM node or an object with a back-reference. Claude should know to avoid this; if it happens, ask Claude to serialize only the specific fields you need rather than the whole object.

completion.headline: M6 complete. Phase 2 done.
completion.body: You can read, write, and validate JSON. Phase 2 — The Language Layer — is complete. Next up: M7 — APIs & HTTP.

steps.title: Read a JSON file
steps.body: You've been working with JSON since M0 — the module files powering this course are JSON. Now look at one directly to see the format in isolation.

commandNotes.what: Python's built-in JSON formatter. Validates the file and pretty-prints it with consistent indentation. No install required.
commandNotes.when: Confirming a JSON file is valid before committing it. Faster than opening it in a browser. Works on any Mac.

commandNotes.what: Shows only the first 40 lines of output. Keeps large files from flooding the terminal.
commandNotes.when: Sampling a large file without printing the whole thing. Combine with tail -40 to see the end.

steps.verify: Both commands produce output. The second command formats consistently — if there's a parse error, Python reports exactly which line.
steps.trouble: If cat ~/mve-academy/data/m0.json gives "No such file or directory" — your local repo is at a different path. Run find ~ -name m0.json 2>/dev/null to locate it.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude generates a JSON config file and you want to verify it's valid before deploying — python3 -m json.tool file.json
A JSON API response is one long line and unreadable — pipe it through python3 -m json.tool for formatted output
Confirming an MVE Academy module file is valid before running Cowork — this is the exact command to run

steps.title: Write JSON by hand
steps.body: The rules are simple and the errors are predictable. Most JSON mistakes are: trailing commas, single quotes, or missing quotes on keys. Write a small JSON file by hand, then validate it.
steps.tryCue: Create this file exactly as shown. Then validate.
steps.verify: Python formats and outputs the file with no errors. You see the nested structure clearly.
steps.trouble: If Python reports a parse error, it will name the line number. Common fix: a trailing comma on the last item in an array or object. Remove it and re-run.
whenYoullReachForThis: Writing a Riffle catch entry manually to test the app's parser before voice transcripts exist
Creating a JSON fixture for testing — a fake but valid API response to develop against before the real API is connected
Editing an MVE Academy module file directly — same validation step applies

steps.title: Parse JSON in JavaScript
steps.body: JSON.parse() converts a JSON string into a JavaScript object. JSON.stringify() does the reverse. These two functions are everywhere — reading API responses, saving state, logging structured data. The common mistake is calling a method on the string before parsing it.

commandNotes.what: Converts a JSON string into a live JavaScript object. Throws a SyntaxError if the string isn't valid JSON.
commandNotes.when: Whenever you receive JSON from an API, a file, or user input — always parse before accessing properties.

commandNotes.what: Converts an object to a JSON string. The null, 2 arguments add 2-space indentation for readability.
commandNotes.when: Logging an object for debugging, saving state to a file, or sending data to an API.

commandNotes.what: Node's synchronous file reader — reads the entire file as a string. Synchronous means it blocks until done, which is fine for small local files.
commandNotes.when: Loading config files, JSON fixtures, or local data at startup. For large files or server code, use the async version.

steps.verify: Output shows the property values, the compact string, and the pretty-printed object. Last two lines show the catch count (2) and first species.
steps.trouble: If you get SyntaxError: Unexpected token from parse — the raw string has invalid JSON. Single quotes instead of double quotes is the most common cause.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude's code calls response.json() after a fetch — that's an async version of JSON.parse(), returning a Promise
An API returns a JSON string and the app fails on .property access — the response wasn't parsed; add JSON.parse()
Logging an object and seeing [object Object] — wrap it in JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2) to see the contents

steps.title: Intentionally break it
steps.body: The fastest way to recognize JSON errors is to cause them on purpose. Each of these introduces a different category of mistake. Run them, read the error messages, remember them.
steps.tryCue: Run each block separately. Read the error each time.
steps.code:
# Trailing comma
node -e "JSON.parse('{\"a\": 1,}')"

# Single quotes
node -e "JSON.parse(\"{'a': 1}\")"

# Unquoted key
node -e "JSON.parse('{a: 1}')"

# Valid — control case
node -e "console.log(JSON.parse('{\"a\": 1}'))"
steps.verify: First three produce SyntaxError: Unexpected token with a position. The fourth outputs { a: 1 }.
whenYoullReachForThis: An API returns a parse error — these are the four categories to check first
Claude generates a JSON config and it fails to load — paste into python3 -m json.tool to identify the line
An MVE Academy module file breaks the Lab Bench — same four failure modes, same fix

steps.title: Install jq (optional but useful)
steps.body: jq is a command-line tool for querying and filtering JSON. Not required, but useful when API responses are large and you want to pull a specific field without writing JavaScript.
steps.code:
brew install jq
cat ~/catch.json | jq '.catches[0].species'
cat ~/catch.json | jq '.catches | length'
cat ~/catch.json | jq '.catches[] | select(.length > 15)'

commandNotes.what: Extract a top-level field from JSON. Dot notation, same as JavaScript.
commandNotes.when: Pulling one field from a large API response without writing a script.

commandNotes.what: Filter an array by a condition. The .[] iterates, select() keeps matching items.
commandNotes.when: Filtering a list of API results from the terminal — checking which catches are over 15 inches without opening a script.

steps.verify: jq '.catches[0].species' outputs "Rainbow Trout". The filter returns the 18-inch Rainbow Trout object.
whenYoullReachForThis: An API response is 200 lines of JSON and you want one field — curl ... | jq '.data.value'
Exploring an unfamiliar API response structure — cat response.json | jq 'keys' shows top-level fields
Verifying a batch of Riffle catch entries — filter by species or length from the terminal

steps.title: Clean up
steps.verify: Both files are gone. Run ls ~/catch.json 2>/dev/null || echo 'Removed' to confirm.
